defect.evidence_quote: when an employee is being investigated for criminal misconduct or breaches of other nonwork-related statutory or regulatory standards
defect.problem: The holding is supported in core, but it is slightly overbroad and imprecise. The opinion frames the privacy locations as office, desk, and file cabinets, not generically files, and it expressly leaves criminal and nonwork-related investigations outside the adopted standard.
defect.proposed_fix: Revise to: Public employees may have a reasonable expectation of privacy in their offices, desks, and file cabinets, subject to the operational realities of the workplace; legitimate work-related, noninvestigatory intrusions and investigations of work-related misconduct are judged by reasonableness under all the circumstances, without a warrant or probable cause, while criminal and nonwork-related investigations are reserved.

reasons: Text states the case presents whether a public employee had a reasonable expectation of privacy in his office, desk, and file cabinets.
Text rejects the argument that public employees can never have a reasonable expectation of privacy in their place of work and ties the inquiry to operational realities.
Text holds that noninvestigatory, work-related intrusions and investigations of work-related misconduct are judged by reasonableness under all the circumstances.
residual_risks: Cached text contains only the O'Connor plurality opinion; controlling-status treatment of the split decision is recorded in lake treatment fields, not independently tested under Lens A.
reviewed.suggested_tightening: Use 'file cabinets' and add the opinion's reservation for criminal and nonwork-related investigations.
